why.support: Young people have rights at work, when renting and with police. Learn where to find them. Learn to read them. Then you can ask for what's fair.
why.core: Young people have rights at work, when renting, and with police. But rights only help if you know them, and if you can **find**, **read** and **use** the information that explains them. Legal information has its own style: definitions, conditions and long nouns. Learn to read it, sum it up, and write a formal request, and you can stand up for yourself.
why.extend: Rights are only useful if you can access them. That means locating authoritative information, interpreting legal-style texts (definitions, conditions, modal verbs and nominalisation), summarising them accurately, and using formal language to assert them. These are literacy skills with real consequences.

articles.title: Know your rights

body.support:
You have rights at work, when renting, and with police.

**Reading rights information.** Look for headings. Look for *If… then…* rules. Say them in your own words.

**At work**

- **Under 15?** Your boss needs a **licence**. In school terms: up to **3 hours a day**, **12 a week**. Not in school hours. Not after **9 pm**.
- At any age: fair pay, a payslip, breaks and a safe workplace.
- In Victoria, not paying workers on purpose is a **crime**.
- Help: **Fair Work Ombudsman**, **Young Workers Centre**.

**Renting**

- Your **bond** goes to the **RTBA**, not the landlord.
- Urgent repair? Call the emergency number.

**With police**

- If police think you broke the law, you must give your real name and address.
- You can say *no comment* to other questions.
- Help: **Victoria Legal Aid**, **Youth Law Australia**.

Something wrong? Write a short, **formal** message.
body.core:
You have rights at work, when you rent, and with police. To use them, you need to find trusted information, read it carefully, and act on it.

**How rights information is written.** Government and legal aid websites use **headings** to split topics. They **define** key words (*a child means a person under 15*). They use **conditions**: *If you're under 15, your employer must…* And they often turn actions into long nouns: *Employment during school hours is prohibited* just means *you can't work during school hours*. Read the condition, then say it in your own words.

**At work**

- If you're **under 15**, your **employer** needs a free **child employment licence**. During school terms, you can work up to **3 hours a day** and **12 hours a week**. You can't work during school hours, or after **9 pm**.
- At any age, you have a right to at least the minimum pay for your job, a payslip, breaks and a safe workplace.
- In Victoria, deliberately underpaying workers has been a **crime** since **July 2021**.
- Help: the **Fair Work Ombudsman**, **Workforce Inspectorate Victoria** and the **Young Workers Centre**.

**When renting**

- Your **bond** must be lodged with the **Residential Tenancies Bond Authority** (RTBA), not kept by the landlord.
- For **urgent** repairs, like a burst pipe or no hot water, call the landlord's or agent's emergency number. They must respond without delay.
- Help: **Consumer Affairs Victoria** and **Tenants Victoria**.

**With police**

- If police believe you've committed an **offence**, you must give your real name and address. Giving false details is an offence.
- You can say *no comment* to other questions.
- If you're under 18, police should not interview you without a parent, guardian or **independent person** there.
- Help: **Victoria Legal Aid** and **Youth Law Australia**.

When something's wrong, write it down: what happened, when, and what you want. A short, **formal**, polite request in writing is often the fastest fix, and it gives you a record.
body.extend:
Young people have rights at work, in rental housing and with police. Using them depends on finding trusted information, understanding it, and acting on it.

**How legal information is written.** Official sources sort content under **headings**. They **define** terms (*a child is a person under 15*). They state rights as **conditions** (*If…, the employer must…*). They also use **nominalisation**, turning actions into nouns (*Employment during school hours is prohibited*). This can hide who must do what. Turning the noun back into an action makes the obligation clear.

**At work**

- Employers of children **under 15** need a free **child employment licence**. In school terms, the limits are **3 hours a day** and **12 hours a week**, never during school hours and not after **9 pm**.
- All employees are entitled to minimum pay for their role, payslips, breaks and a safe workplace.
- Deliberate underpayment (wage theft) has been a **criminal offence** in Victoria since **1 July 2021**.
- Support: the **Fair Work Ombudsman**, **Workforce Inspectorate Victoria** and the **Young Workers Centre**.

**In rental housing**

- **Bonds** must be lodged with the **Residential Tenancies Bond Authority** (RTBA).
- Urgent repairs must be responded to without delay.
- Support: **Consumer Affairs Victoria** and **Tenants Victoria**.

**With police**

- If police believe you've committed an **offence**, you must provide your correct name and address; false details are an offence.
- You may decline to answer other questions (*no comment*).
- People under 18 should not be interviewed without a parent, guardian or **independent person** present.
- Support: **Victoria Legal Aid** and **Youth Law Australia**.

When asserting a right, put it in writing: the facts, the relevant rule and a clear, polite request. **Formal** written communication creates a record and is often the most effective first step.

caseStudies.title: The canteen kids

body.support:
In **2023**, a business ran canteens at footy clubs in Melbourne. It hired lots of kids.

A government group checked. It found the business:

- had no **licence** to hire 10 of the kids
- hired **3 kids** who were under **13**, the youngest age allowed
- gave kids **too many hours** in school term.

In **2024**, the owner was fined **$4,000** by a court.

The government said kids working 8-hour days was not OK. School comes first.

The rules protect young workers. But only if people know them.
body.core:
In **2023**, a business ran canteens at sports clubs in **Brighton** and **Elsternwick**, in Melbourne. It employed lots of kids.

The **Wage Inspectorate Victoria** checked. (It's now called **Workforce Inspectorate Victoria**.) It found the business had:

- employed **10 children** without a child employment permit or licence, on **64** occasions
- employed **3 children** under the minimum working age of **13**, on **20** occasions
- given **10 children** more hours than allowed during the school term, on **56** occasions.

In **2024**, the owner pleaded **guilty** in court. They were fined **$4,000**. The magistrate said the fine would have been **$10,000** if they hadn't pleaded guilty early.

The Commissioner said kids working days of up to **8 hours** was not OK. School must come first for kids that age.

These rules protect young workers. But they only work if workers, parents and bosses know them.
body.extend:
In **2023**, a business that ran canteens at sports clubs in **Brighton** and **Elsternwick** employed a number of children.

**Wage Inspectorate Victoria** investigated and laid charges. (It was renamed **Workforce Inspectorate Victoria** in December 2025.) In **2024**, the owner pleaded **guilty** in the Melbourne Magistrates' Court to 23 charges, including:

- **10 children** worked with no permit or licence, on **64** occasions.
- **3 children** were under the minimum working age of **13**, on **20** occasions.
- **10 children** worked more than the school-term limit, on **56** occasions.

The court fined the owner **$4,000** and imposed a good behaviour bond. The magistrate said the fine would have been **$10,000** without the early guilty plea.

The Commissioner said children working days of up to **8 hours** was unacceptable. School must be the priority.

The case shows how exact rules protect young workers: licences, minimum ages and hour limits. It also shows why the exact wording of a rule matters.

model.text:
**Subject:** Unpaid trial shift on 3 May

Dear Mr Carter,

I am writing about the trial shift I worked at your café on Saturday 3 May, from 8 am to 1 pm.

I served customers and worked the register for five hours. I have not been paid for this time.

The Fair Work Ombudsman says a trial must be paid if it goes beyond showing your skills. I believe five hours of real work should be paid.

Could you please pay me for the five hours by Friday 16 May?

Yours sincerely,
Lena Novak

teacher.overview: The boss level of Get Sorted. Students learn to locate authoritative rights information (government and legal aid sites) and read its legal style: headings, definitions, conditions (*if…, must…*), numerical limits and nominalisation. Content covers Victorian child employment rules for under-15s, pay rights and wage theft laws, renting basics (bonds and urgent repairs) and dealing with police (name and address, right to silence, independent persons). Students summarise their rights on a rights card, practise shifting from casual to formal language, and write a formal email asserting a right. The case study is a 2024 Melbourne Magistrates' Court case over children working in sports club canteens.
prep: Print the key official pages (child employment rules, Victoria Legal Aid's young people and police page, Consumer Affairs Victoria renting basics) in case sites are blocked.
Check rules are current: the regulator was renamed Workforce Inspectorate Victoria in December 2025, and laws change.
Have support contacts ready: Young Workers Centre, Youth Law Australia, Victoria Legal Aid, Tenants Victoria.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Reading rights
steps: **Hook (10 min):** the canteen shift. Legal or not? How would you find out?
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** headings, definitions, conditions, long nouns; model on the rights page.
**Read (15 min):** article and Check your reading.
**Annotate (10 min):** Anatomy of a rights page.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Applying rights
steps: **Legal or not? (15 min).** Students name the rule for each card.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Summing up
steps: **My rights card (30 min),** using official websites.
**Make it formal (20 min).** Discuss: how does language change with who you're talking to?

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Standing up
steps: **Model (10 min):** write a formal email together.
**Final mission (25 min):** stand up for a right.
**Level Up, reflect (15 min):** quick check; request sign-off.

keyPoints: Find rights information on government and legal aid sites.
Read legal style: headings, definitions, conditions, limits; unpack nominalisation into who must do what.
Under 15 (Vic): employer needs a free licence; school term max 3 hours a day and 12 a week; not in school hours or after 9 pm. Minimum working age 13 for most jobs.
All ages: minimum pay, payslips, breaks, a safe workplace; wage theft is a crime in Victoria (since 1 July 2021).
Renting: bonds go to the RTBA; urgent repairs need a response without delay.

Police: give your real name and address if they believe you've committed an offence; you can say no comment to other questions; under 18s should have a parent, guardian or independent person at an interview.
Assert rights in writing: facts, rule, polite request.

support: Fewer sort cards and table rows.
Teacher's printouts for the rights card; two scenarios and starters for the email.
extend: Cite the rule and its source in the email.
Write a speech or post raising the issue (Level Up).

Creates a formal email with developed, organised ideas for its purpose and audience (final mission).
Adjusts language for formality and social distance (Make it formal, final mission).
Interprets and evaluates legal information and a real enforcement case (case study, Check your reading).
Level Up: creates a text raising an issue, with deliberate language choices for an audience.
Explains and unpacks nominalisation in legal texts (Unpack it, annotation, Level Up).

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** up to 3 hours a day and 12 a week, not in school hours, not after 9 pm, and the employer needs a licence. Your real name and address; you can say no comment to other questions. Help: Fair Work Ombudsman, Workforce Inspectorate Victoria, Young Workers Centre, Consumer Affairs Victoria, Tenants Victoria, Victoria Legal Aid, Youth Law Australia.

**Rights page:** 1 heading; 2 definition (who it's about); 3 condition (employer must hold a licence); 4 limits; 5 nominalisation (you can't work in school hours); 6 next step (where to report).

**Sort:** Jack 4 hours — not legal; Mia holidays 6 hours with licence — legal; Ava 9:30 pm — not legal; Leo fake name — not legal; Zoe no comment — legal; landlord keeps bond — not legal.

**Unpack (samples):** it's an offence to give police a false name; the landlord must lodge the bond with the RTBA; employers must not pay less than the minimum rate; if you don't follow the rules, you may be penalised.

**Case study:** no permit or licence; children under the minimum age of 13; too many hours in school term. Questions: Does my employer have a child employment licence? How many hours will I work, and when?

**Make it formal (samples):** I haven't yet been paid for my shift on Saturday 14 March; could you please arrange this by Friday?; Thank you for your help / Kind regards; I'm concerned this may not meet the requirements.

realityCheck: **Laws change.** Check every rule against the official pages before teaching. This course was written in 2026, after the regulator's name changed.
**Police can be a sensitive topic.** Some students, and their families, have had bad experiences. Keep it factual and focused on rights and where to get help.
**Some students are already in unsafe or illegal jobs.** Make it easy and anonymous to ask for help; the Young Workers Centre and Youth Law Australia give free, confidential advice.
**This isn't legal advice.** Tell students that for their own situation, they should contact Victoria Legal Aid or Youth Law Australia.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's the natural finale to Get Sorted, using reading, summarising and formal writing for things that matter to students right now.

levels.extend: Adds bond and independent person to the vocabulary, a quiz question on the case, an email citing the rule and its source, and Level Ups writing a speech raising the issue and analysing nominalisation.
